---
title: "Ruby for non-Rubyists"
---

You already write software, so you don't need a Ruby tutorial. You need the
short list of places where Ruby's punctuation and idiom differ from whatever
language you think in, because those are the only places an example in this book
will stop you. Sonic Pi puts a music language on top of Ruby and the lessons use
a deliberately small slice of the host language. That slice is what follows,
roughly in the order you'll meet it.

One reading habit helps more than any single rule here. When an example looks
musically clear and syntactically strange, find the shape of its data first,
then come back and decode the punctuation.

## Symbols are interned names, not strings

`:c4` is a *symbol*: an immutable, interned identifier. If your background is
Lisp, you already know them. If it's Python or JavaScript, think of a string
that's guaranteed unique in memory and never gets mutated or formatted.

```ruby
play :c4          # symbol
play 60           # the same note as an integer
```

Sonic Pi names notes, synths, and scales with symbols, which is why the leading
colon shows up on nearly every page. Symbols behave like ordinary values: they
sit in arrays and serve as hash keys.

One thing here is not Ruby. Inside Sonic Pi's runtime, `:c4 + 12` gives you the
C an octave up, because the music layer converts the note name before doing the
arithmetic. Plain Ruby won't add an integer to an arbitrary symbol, so don't
carry that trick outside the buffer.

## Arrays

Zero-indexed, negative indexes count from the end, ranges slice. No surprises.

```ruby
notes = [60, 62, 64, 65]
notes[0]       # => 60
notes[-1]      # => 65
notes[1..2]    # => [62, 64]
```

`+` concatenates and `rotate` moves values from the front to the back, which is
exactly what the modes chapter needs.

```ruby
[60, 64] + [67]         # => [60, 64, 67]
[0, 2, 4, 5].rotate(1)  # => [2, 4, 5, 0]
```

Watch the trailing `!`. By convention it marks the mutating twin of a method:
`sort` returns a new array, `sort!` rearranges the receiver. Score data in this
book stays immutable, so the non-mutating form is the one you'll see.

## Hashes carry the event schema

A hash gives names to related values, which beats parallel arrays the moment a
note needs a start time, a duration, and an amplitude. Event keys are symbols,
and `note: 60` is shorthand for `:note => 60`.

```ruby
event = {note: 60, start: 0, duration: 1, amp: 0.8}
event[:note]            # => 60
event.fetch(:duration)  # => 1
event.fetch(:pan, 0)    # => 0 when :pan is absent
```

Reach for `fetch` when a missing key is a bug, or when you want the default
visible at the call site. Square brackets return `nil` for a missing key, and
`nil` will happily travel three functions downstream before anything complains.
That's how a typo in `:duraton` turns into a silent renderer.

## Blocks

A block is an anonymous function attached to a method call. Ruby spells a long
one `do ... end` and a one-liner in braces, with parameters between vertical
bars. Read the next example as "four times, with the current count called `i`."

```ruby
4.times do |i|
  play 60 + i
  sleep 0.5
end
```

The block isn't an argument in the ordinary sense. It's a second channel the
method can yield to, which is why `4.times` needs no callback syntax and no
lambda.

## each and map

One Ruby distinction shapes the musical model, so it's worth being precise about
it. `each` walks the values for an effect, such as playing a note, and returns
the receiver. `map` transforms each value and returns a new array, which is what
a transposition is.

```ruby
[60, 64, 67].each { |n| play n; sleep 0.5 }
[60, 64, 67].map  { |n| n + 12 }              # => [72, 76, 79]
```

If a score change vanishes without a trace, check that you didn't write `each`
where the result mattered.

Block parameters destructure, which is how every score walker in the book reads
pairs:

```ruby
[[:c4, 1], [:e4, 0.5]].each do |pitch, duration|
  play pitch
  sleep duration
end
```

Three more enumerable methods appear later:

```ruby
[60, 62, 64].each_cons(2).to_a  # => [[60, 62], [62, 64]]
[60, 64, 67].zip([1, 1, 2])     # => [[60, 1], [64, 1], [67, 2]]
[1, 2, 3].sum                   # => 6
```

`each_cons(2)` hands you adjacent pairs, which is what interval and
voice-leading checks are made of. `zip` aligns parallel arrays by index. `sum`
does the bar-duration assertions.

## Conditions

`if` is an expression, and a short condition can trail the statement it governs.

```ruby
quality = interval == 4 ? :major : :minor
play note if note

if duration <= 0
  raise "duration must be positive"
end
```

Here's the rule that bites people arriving from C, Python, or JavaScript: only
`false` and `nil` are falsy. Zero is true. Empty string, true. Empty array,
true. That matters constantly here, because pitch class 0 is C and `play note if
note` is a real guard against a rest.

`case` reads well over symbolic music data:

```ruby
offsets = case quality
          when :major then [0, 4, 7]
          when :minor then [0, 3, 7]
          else raise "unknown quality"
          end
```

## Keyword arguments

Trailing `name: value` pairs are keyword arguments, and Sonic Pi uses them for
everything that shapes a sound once the pitch is settled.

```ruby
play :c4, amp: 0.7, release: 2, cutoff: 90
```

## Defining functions

Sonic Pi wraps Ruby's `def` in a call to `define`, which registers the function
with the runtime so it's reachable inside threads and across repeated runs.

```ruby
define :play_phrase do |score, transpose: 0|
  score.each { |pitch, duration| play pitch + transpose; sleep duration }
end
```

Arguments before the keyword section are positional. A keyword with a default is
optional, one without a default is required, and the last expression evaluated
becomes the return value. Explicit `return` is rare in Ruby and you'll almost
never see it here.

```ruby
define :transpose do |notes, by:|
  notes.map { |n| n + by }
end

transpose([60, 64, 67], by: 12)
```

Put every definition above its first call. Sonic Pi does remember a named
definition between runs, and that's precisely the trap: an example that only
works because of what your buffer remembers is an example you can't hand to
anyone else.

## Rings

A ring is Sonic Pi's circular sequence. Index past the end of an array and Ruby
gives you `nil`; index past the end of a ring and it wraps, so `ring(1, 2, 3)[4]`
is `2`. That suits a performance pattern that outlasts its source material.

```ruby
notes = ring(:c4, :e4, :g4)
8.times { |i| play notes[i]; sleep 0.5 }   # cycles, no bounds error
```

Sonic Pi adds `tick` and `look`, thread-local counters over a ring. `tick`
advances and returns; `look` reads without advancing.

```ruby
notes = ring(:c4, :e4, :g4)
6.times do
  play notes.tick
  sleep 0.5
end
```

The book uses `tick` for repeating performance patterns and an explicit index
for transformations where the position carries meaning. An explicit index is
easier to print when several rings advance at different rates.

## Numbers

Pitch arithmetic is integer arithmetic; beat arithmetic often isn't. Ruby's `/`
truncates on two integers, so `2 / 3` is `0` and your triplet disappears. Write
`2.0 / 3`. Modulo does the other reduction you need constantly, folding an
unbounded note address into a pitch class or an event count into a pattern slot.

```ruby
61 % 12       # => 1, the pitch class C-sharp or D-flat
2.0 / 3       # => 0.6666666666666666
13 % 4        # => 1, the second slot in a four-step pattern
```

Floating-point duration sums accumulate small errors. When you check a bar of
fractional events, compare within a tolerance and don't demand exact equality.

## Threads and shared state

`in_thread` and `live_loop` run musical lines concurrently under Sonic Pi's
deterministic scheduler. Local variables are captured when the thread starts.
For coordination between long-lived loops, `cue` and `sync` pass messages, and
`set` and `get` hold named state for values that genuinely have to change.

Prefer messages and immutable score data over shared mutable arrays. A live loop
reading an array while another writes it is much harder to reason about than two
loops that start from one cue and read stable data.

## The short list of things that trip you up

Integer division truncates, so spell a triplet `2.0 / 3`. Only `nil` and `false`
are falsy, so a pitch class of 0 is a true value. Symbols and strings are
different types, and Sonic Pi wants symbols for musical names. A method name
ending in `?` calls like any other; the punctuation is a promise about the
return value, not syntax. And the last expression is the return value, which
means a stray `puts` at the end of a function returns `nil` to your caller.
